what_it_does: Large AI language models are increasingly used to turn spoken audio into text (automatic speech recognition, or ASR), but they generate words one at a time in a slow sequential chain. Speculative decoding is a technique that uses a small, fast model to guess several words ahead, then checks those guesses with the large model in a single step — accepting correct guesses and discarding wrong ones, net effect being faster output. This paper argues that ASR is a special case where the audio signal strongly steers what words come next, meaning a small ASR model and a large one tend to agree on output far more often than in free-form text generation. SpecASR exploits this insight with three additions: it adjusts how many words to guess at a time based on how well things are going, reuses guesses from previous moments in the audio stream, and builds a branching tree of possible word sequences so more guesses can be checked at once.
